where ${C}_{1}$ is oriented counterclockwise and ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](images/0d/0de833fcc39b6295418c1558cf1187774db7b4ada1d697f2dcac8c35858563df.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =10-4-2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "39c00f45-8518-5817-af27-2a3b132c427a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441622}} {:db/id 17592186441619 :step/content {:db/id 17592186441617 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "68a479bb-7541-5424-a117-bc163a220ec5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24\pi " :db/id 17592186441596} {:answer/id #uuid "8eb606cd-8859-52ad-923b-4174c43b9bc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "25\pi " :db/id 17592186441599} {:answer/id #uuid "bab36efc-1119-58ba-bc4b-a7d41daed2a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "40\pi " :db/id 17592186441602} {:answer/id #uuid "d102eb68-b278-588e-9ae4-718a08bc02d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\pi " :db/id 17592186441604} {:answer/id #uuid "fbd69b33-186c-5c7d-b495-4a5c8ed20698" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30\pi " :db/id 17592186441609}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186441604} :answer-field/id #uuid "25ffc2c7-e514-54e6-8c7b-600c1de04088" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186441612}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "93b19a79-b263-5685-8630-5024a89d98bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-126893" :question/problem "![](images/df/df52e2add706a17bf93236cdaa04582932b6c799d4a88a3e194a3a3788c816ff.png)

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=4y$ and $Q(x,y)=5x.$ So, 

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=5.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}4y\,dx+5x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-4)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\text{Area}(D) \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 4}{2}-\frac{2\cdot 2}{2} \\  & =8-2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ae2af08-c3b9-5a97-9f39-1c8f6e552dc4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441619}} {:db/id 17592186441621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186441616 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12bc592f-463c-5b10-94de-5b44d176d00d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{89}{3}" :db/id 17592186441590} {:answer/id #uuid "1e63af1d-9e8f-51ce-b89b-69668a98103f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186441591} {:answer/id #uuid "6f81656c-ec2b-52fd-99b0-096af9bbcd54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-14" :db/id 17592186441597} {:answer/id #uuid "e220a614-c017-51de-896b-5544add5e4e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186441606} {:answer/id #uuid "fbafbae6-9a9a-5e89-b7aa-04db6e10b82c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{52}{3}" :db/id 17592186441608}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186441608} :answer-field/id #uuid "25134893-42bb-5ae1-bdf7-77b092bdf96e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186441611}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "311f57fc-3b6c-595d-a8b9-91e8d4d5d656" :question/math-academy-id "q-126947" :question/problem "![](images/82/823ab320e0f1426b846c7bf561b977ac6458c80d235aabdc5647a7db07c4cb74.png)

where $D$ is the region shown above." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2x{y}^{3}+{x}^{5}$ and $Q(x,y)=5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=6x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=10x{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(2x{y}^{3}+{x}^{5})\,dx+(5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}10x{y}^{2}-6x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 2,-2\le y\le 1\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,-1\le y\le 0\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}4x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-2}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}4x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{0}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-2}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =(8-2)\cdot (\frac{1}{3}-(-\frac{8}{3}))-(2-0)\cdot (0-(-\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =6\cdot 3-2\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =18-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{52}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2y$ and $Q(x,y)=4x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}2y\,dx+4x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (6\cdot 4-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (24-4) \\  & =2\cdot 20 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1b31cf93-d5e4-581a-abf0-1f4ce4b0318a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498614}} {:db/id 17592186498614 :step/content {:db/id 17592186369462 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5d7cf9a0-e8a9-528c-9faf-b2259025de3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186369464} {:answer/id #uuid "ce1af42a-4bf9-5730-a278-44c2bcb271c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "19" :db/id 17592186369465} {:answer/id #uuid "26f52db4-19ad-52bc-bdea-a43ddccabe76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186369466} {:answer/id #uuid "74b55cd4-e132-5c25-af68-783e5644f0be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186369467} {:answer/id #uuid "5901a191-1792-51d7-92cf-8ae7fe658d89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186369468}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186369468} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0c368b0-4e71-50a8-b81a-cf6d68ab083b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186369463}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ca63e980-b1ab-5e66-b1ce-ccb3144f7558" :question/math-academy-id "q-126862" :question/problem "![](images/49/49b14da54c952d0585f7aa894d618838ddc91beb65216e0c18c014ba5ad268d7.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=9,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-4,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-6,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ is oriented counterclockwise and ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](images/a8/a8e93055fb9a460ab7757475c9c381c191204eae72231921da870b8d727bf988.png)

Therefore, we have

:question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{1}{x+5}=\frac{1}{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{1}=\frac{3}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
x+5=3
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =3 \\ x+5-5 & =3-5 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059708 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059521 :question/id #uuid "3ae175a8-7654-57c8-b5d8-33d7892b7a24" :question/math-academy-id "e-4235"} :knowledge-point/id {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{2}{3x+2}=-\frac{4}{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503661 :question/id #uuid "1a235d31-7002-5190-8de9-b78ca920ac5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-67425"} {:db/id 17592186503729 :question/id #uuid "Solve the equation $-\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{1}{x-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{x-1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $4.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{4x-4}{4}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (\frac{x-2}{-4}) & =(-4)\cdot \frac{4x-4}{4} \\ x-2 & =-4x+4 \\ x+4x & =4+2 \\ 5x & =6 \\ (\frac{1}{5})\cdot (5x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ x & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048895} {:db/id 17592186048994} {:db/id 17592186049860} {:db/id 17592186050474} {:db/id 17592186050818 :topic/id #uuid "68e64e22-0e3c-5eac-8837-c36b21dd36c0" "Solve the inequality $-9<-3x+8<-5.$" :question/worked-solution "We isolate $x$ by applying the addition and multiplication principles, as usual. 

First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9 & <-3x+8<-5 \\ -9-8 & <-3x+8-8<-5-8 \\ -17 & <-3x<-13\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-3.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs.

$$
\begin{aligned}-17 & <-3x<-13 \\ \frac{-17}{-3} & >\frac{-3x}{-3}>\frac{-13}{-3} \\ \frac{17}{3} & >x>\frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

The solution can be written as $\frac{17}{3}>x>\frac{13}{3}$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
\frac{13}{3}<x<\frac{17}{3}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186069228 :question/id #uuid "b61c5dfe-34c0-5830-8c59-cd20d813f4bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-3070"} {:db/id 17592186290303 :question/id #uuid First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & \le -2x+3\le 5 \\ -5-3 & \le -2x+3-3\le 5-3 \\ -8 & \le -2x\le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-2.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & \le -2x\le 2 \\ \frac{-8}{-2} & \ge \frac{-2x}{-2}\ge \frac{2}{-2} \\ \frac{8}{2} & \ge x\ge -\frac{2}{2} \\ 4 & \ge x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution can be written as $4\ge x\ge -1$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
-1\le x\le 4
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C+m∠D & ={360}^{∘} \\ x+{90}^{∘}+3x+6x & ={360}^{∘} \\ 10x+{90}^{∘} & ={360}^{∘} \\ 10x & ={270}^{∘} \\ x & ={27}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠C & =3x \\  & =3({27}^{∘}) \\  & ={81}^{∘}.\end{aligned}

To calculate this, we find the meteor's mass after $2$ minutes, and we subtract its mass after $3$ minutes. So we need to evaluate

$$
m(2)-m(3).
$$

The mass of the meteor after $t=2$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}m(2) & =20\cdot (0.4)^{2} \\  & =20\cdot 0.16 \\  & =3.2.\end{aligned}
$$

The mass of the meteor after $t=3$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}m(3) & =20\cdot (0.4)^{3} \\  & =20\cdot 0.064 \\  & =1.28.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total mass lost between the second and third minute is

$$
m(2)-m(3)=3.2-1.28=1.92.
$$

Therefore, the meteor's mass decreased by $1.92$ metric tons between the second and third minutes."} {:db/id 17592186115869 :question/id #uuid "977226b8-4490-5f1a-950f-1ae37c9b67f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-45730"} {:db/id 17592186508972 :question/id #uuid "bce8526b-2382-5fd4-882b-274b4364bd61" :question/math-academy-id "q-112525"} {:db/id 17592186508980 :question/id #uuid "d33dc350-97af-5862-9547-76e026eaf801" :question/math-academy-id "q-64120"} {:db/id 17592186557278 :question/id #uuid "8c286c29-c804-5f9e-952f-d64fbcc60ae3" :question/math-academy-id "q-45713" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "120cc5f5-b994-5fe7-879c-93dded23b4f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "46\,900" :db/id 17592186556465} {:answer/id #uuid "62f35678-61c9-5979-beb7-a4d92e98be00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "46\,875" :db/id 17592186556656} {:answer/id #uuid "8af9a23c-445a-5275-9661-7299cac973d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "40\,875" :db/id 17592186556762} {:answer/id #uuid "9ee33d95-d119-584c-b8ee-7dac64f9c29c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50\,000" :db/id 17592186556817} {:answer/id #uuid "fb544b2f-30e9-5368-a619-27b767c38ae4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48\,675" :db/id 17592186557052}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186556656} :answer-field/id #uuid "b9cb964d-8a8c-59d6-bbd2-2c379e559c33" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186557169}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The population $C(t)$ of condors in the Andes is given by $C(t)=1\,000\,000\cdot (0.25)^{t}$, where $t$ is the time, in decades, since the last census. To calculate this, we find the population after $2$ decades, and we subtract the population after $3$ decades. So we need to evaluate

$$
C(2)-C(3).
$$

The number of condors after $t=2$ decades is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}C(2) & =1\,000\,000\cdot (0.25)^{2} \\  & =1\,000\,000\cdot 0.062\,5 \\  & =62\,500.\end{aligned}
$$

The number of condors after $t=3$ decades is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}C(3) & =1\,000\,000\cdot (0.25)^{3} \\  & =1\,000\,000\cdot 0.015\,625 \\  & =15\,625.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the number of condors lost between the second and third decades is

$$
C(3)-C(2)=62\,500-15\,625=46\,875.
$$

Therefore, $46\,875$ condors vanished between the second and third decades."} {:db/id 17592186115384 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186114949 :question/id #uuid kept at a fixed distance apart, varies directly with the **square** of the charge $q$ of each particle, measured in coulombs $(C).$ If the electrostatic force is $8\,976\,N$ when the charges are $2\,C,$ then express $F$ in terms of $q.$

$F=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The electrostatic force $F$ is directly proportional to the square of the charge $q,$ so we have

$$
F=k{q}^{2},
$$

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $F=8\,976\,\text{N}$ when $q=2\,\text{C}.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8\,976 & =k\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 8\,976 & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{8\,976}{4} & =k \\ 2\,244 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our direct variation equation is

$$
F=2\,244{q}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186571398 :question/id #uuid "52c4a416-f053-5e55-99b6-12fd0ef1b322" :question/math-academy-id "q-120299" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b0f61ca-4b31-5d02-b3fa-da62506bb922" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186570909} {:answer/id #uuid "178a11f1-2e2f-512c-81ef-7ba747eb04b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi" :db/id 17592186570924} {:answer/id #uuid "31844f5d-e1c6-58a5-911d-752c2c6738db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186570969} {:answer/id #uuid "34146648-0aef-5194-b0bd-b28640147dea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi" :db/id 17592186570972} {:answer/id #uuid "4841b2db-6473-515a-b60c-cb4143294f92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi" :db/id 17592186571005}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186570972} :answer-field/id #uuid "4782ff3c-c734-5dad-88e3-9bed03473528" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186571309}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The surface $S,$ in square centimeters, of a cylinder whose height equals the radius of its base varies directly with the **square** of its radius $r,$ measured in centimeters. $$
S=k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $S=16\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}$ when $r=2\,\text{cm}.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16\pi  & =k\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 16\pi  & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{16\pi }{4} & =k \\ 4\pi  & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the constant of variation is $k=4\pi .$"} {:db/id 17592186571412 :question/id #uuid "6bd84e69-7c5f-5a4e-bce4-f665a1006214" :question/math-academy-id "q-52005" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1897ea72-c13e-5fd4-8083-32c921ead598" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186570927} {:answer/id #uuid "4786e8d1-90b1-5d13-9ebd-a4ddaedea0e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186571003} {:answer/id #uuid "58ba7898-216c-5d88-b22b-f355ac55120b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186571031} {:answer/id #uuid "82b7408e-0165-58fb-9ffe-29dd90fb32bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186571094} {:answer/id #uuid "d611d837-c607-55f1-84f6-82a363b4fcc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186571224}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186571224} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf2bf7fa-473d-5f46-831b-f02037509aa6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186571356}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The distance $d$, in meters, a falling body travels after being released from rest varies directly with the **square** of the time $t,$ measured in seconds, since the body was released. $10$ girls, then how many members does the club have in total?" :question/worked-solution "We start with the ratio $2:1$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{2}{1}
$$

In this fraction, the numerator represents the number of girls, and the denominator represents the number of boys.

We can make a numerator of $10$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5:$

$$
\frac{2\times 5}{1\times 5}=\frac{10}{5}
$$

Therefore, there are $10$ girls and $5$ boys in the club. So the total number of members is

3756} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180522 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180739 :tutorial/content "When dealing with sums or differences of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same algebraic expression under the square root symbol $\sqrt{\phantom 0}.$ This is similar to collecting like terms in a linear expression.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{x}
$$

We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{x}-3\sqrt{x} & = \\ (5-3)\sqrt{x} & = \\ 2\sqrt{x} & \end{aligned}
$$

We *cannot* combine terms when the expressions under the radical are different. For example, the expression

$$
5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{y}
$$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt x$ and $\sqrt y.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "deda60a8-4b35-50ac-a71c-d3f884aa8e1d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5971 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9e6999c1-79fe-5006-91df-3c25468791e3" :step/math-academy-id 36452 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180549}} {:db/id 17592186180523 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179751 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179619 :question/id #uuid "213ad0ee-813b-5a4b-8926-5fbd1aed4906" :question/math-academy-id "e-9723"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "79a1c2e0-4183-58c6-ac88-0a4856b751a2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048170}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180162} {:db/id 17592186180179} {:db/id 17592186501140} {:db/id 17592186501154} {:db/id 17592186501180} {:db/id 17592186501203} {:db/id 17592186502098} {:db/id 17592186502138} {:db/id 17592186563736}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Sums of Radicals with Cube Roots"} :step/id #uuid "145c40ab-6bce-539c-acfa-6819834eff82" :step/math-academy-id 36453} {:db/id 17592186180536 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180749 :tutorial/content "Recall that the product rule for radicals states that

$$
\sqrt{a\cdot b} = \sqrt{a}\cdot \sqrt{b}
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are nonnegative.

We can use the product rule for radicals to simplify some expressions. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "30549c94-702e-5e00-8cdc-4a050a34243f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6012 :tutorial/title "The Product Rule for Radicals"} :step/id #uuid "e61e6895-553c-5528-9f47-4ce31a87b2fc" :step/math-academy-id 36694 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180550}} {:db/id 17592186180537 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180750 :tutorial/content "We can simplify cube root expressions in the same way as with square roots.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
4\sqrt[3]x - 2\sqrt[3] x
$$

We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\sqrt[3]{x}-2\sqrt[3]{x} & = \\ (4-2)\sqrt[3]{x} & = \\ 2\sqrt[3]{x} & \end{aligned}
$$

 

As with square roots, we *cannot* combine terms when the expressions under the radical are different. For example, the expression

$$
\sqrt[3]{x-1} + \sqrt[3]{x+1}
$$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt[3]{x-1}$ and $\sqrt[3]{x+1}.$

Finally, it is not possible to combine square root and cube root terms, even if the numbers under the radical symbol are the same! For example, the expression

$$
2\sqrt x + \sqrt[3] x

![](images/84/848e64be2b80b78d88da42473f6778d4012f7ec52ae6950f4ca3635b5b154ca6.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f8e3ddf-673b-5e4a-9d61-f8a2c682ee36" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3986 :tutorial/title "Circular Segments and Sectors"} {:activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186106588} :activity/id #uuid "2af93617-2850-5d80-8e89-a45566d1d99b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049223 :topic/id #uuid "e4ba6b67-ce78-5f37-b120-6055b0e97c6c" :topic/math-academy-id 1319} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107137 :tutorial/content "The sum of the interior angles of *any* triangle equals $180^\circ.$

![](images/fc/fcc21c5e13ab095da35eeca128e3a82a075d649e205aa0e1683b6ab0e4a4cc4c.png)

As it turns out, there is a general rule for the sum of the interior angles that applies to all polygons:

*The sum of the interior angles of a polygon with $n$ sides equals $180^\circ \cdot (n-2).$*

For example, every triangle has ${\color{blue}3}$ sides. Let's substitute $n={\color{blue}3}$ into the formula to check that it works:

$$
\begin{aligned}{180}^{∘}\cdot (n-2) & ={180}^{∘}\cdot (3-2) \\  & ={180}^{∘}\cdot 1 \\  & ={180}^{∘}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula tells us that the sum of the interior angles of a triangle equals $180^\circ,$ which we know is correct.

Every quadrilateral has $n={\color{blue}4}$ sides. Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{180}^{∘}\cdot (n-2) & ={180}^{∘}\cdot (4-2) \\  & ={180}^{∘}\cdot 2 \\  & ={360}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula tells us that the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral equals $360^\circ.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{180}^{∘}\cdot (n-2) & =1\,{260}^{∘} \\ n-2 & =\frac{1\,{260}^{∘}}{{180}^{∘}} \\ n-2 & =7 \\ n & =9\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠M+m∠N+m∠P+m∠O & ={360}^{∘} \\ {104}^{∘}+(10x-{4}^{∘})+{104}^{∘}+{76}^{∘} & ={360}^{∘} \\ 10x+{280}^{∘} & ={360}^{∘} \\ 10x & ={80}^{∘} \\ x & ={8}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

:tutorial/content "A good example of a direct variation model is the distance an object travels when moving at a constant rate. In this case, the corresponding direct variation equation is 

$$
d=vt,
$$

 

where 

- $d$ is the total distance traveled by the object,

- $t$ is the total time that the object has been traveling, and,

- $v$ is the constant of proportionality, called the **speed** of the object.

For instance, if an object travels a distance of $24\,\textrm m$ in $4$ seconds, then we can substitute $d=24\,\textrm m$ and $t=4\,\textrm s$ into the above equation and solve for $v,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}24 & =v\cdot 4 \\ \frac{24}{4} & =v \\ 6 & =v\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation that relates $d$ and $t$ is

$$
d=6t.
$$

 

One thing to note is that the constant of proportionality $v = 6$ also has units. So let's work out what these units are.

Since we have

$$
d = vt,
$$

it follows that

$$
v = \dfrac{d}{t}.
$$

So, the units of $v$ are

$$
\dfrac{\textrm m}{\textrm s} = \textrm m / \textrm s.
$$

Therefore, the constant of proportionality (including its unit) is $v = 6\, \textrm m / \textrm s.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dcda3158-97b6-5a4a-b062-3803a3db7b26" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "577c6468-9f0e-55fb-84fc-17fcc4e6bca8" :step/math-academy-id 196782 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139354}} {:db/id 17592186139354 :step/content {:db/id 17592186138430 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186138166 :question/id #uuid "f01f91de-9010-5429-ba83-faaf90c866d7" :question/math-academy-id "e-14086"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a35a2fee-a1a5-59aa-9390-f73d2898320c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049092} {:db/id 17592186049141}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186138736} {:db/id 17592186138826} {:db/id 17592186499522} {:db/id 17592186499543} {:db/id 17592186541112}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Constant of Variation"} :step/id #uuid "fd7ad040-afed-5ba6-ad72-f3ed0909fc54" :step/math-academy-id 196783 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139355}} {:db/id 17592186139355 :step/content {:db/id 17592186138431 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186138168 :question/id #uuid "f1408bad-ae5c-55fb-b78e-60ee0d8a1ca0" :question/math-academy-id "e-14088"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7df32abc-07bd-5213-a838-50e893ff5759" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186138664} {:db/id 17592186138738} {:db/id 17592186499547}] :knowledge-point/title "Modeling With Direct Variation"} :step/id #uuid "d2efc257-0a27-570d-a356-98d12f63e6c2" :step/math-academy-id 196786 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139356}} {:db/id 17592186139356 :step/content {:db/id 17592186139719 :tutorial/content "When modeling proportional relationships, we sometimes find that a quantity $y$ varies directly with the *square* of a second quantity $x.$ In such cases, we write

$$
y = kx^2.
$$

For example, consider a circle of radius $r,$ measured in centimeters.

![](images/fa/fad3151a754d96d3e4ad97fa812ce7087601cebe7c4ab00f7b3c8cd603b140c0.png)

It can be shown that the area $A,$ measured in square meters, of a circle varies directly with the *square* of the radius $r.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
A = k r^2.

For instance, suppose that the ratio of boys to girls in the fifth grade is $3: 4.$ If there are $15$ boys, how many students are there in total?

Notice that the "total number of students" doesn't appear in the ratio. However, we can find the number of students by adding the total number of boys and the number of girls.

We start with the ratio ${\color{blue}3}:{\color{red}4}$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}}{{\color{red}4}}
$$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}\times 5}{{\color{red}4}\times 5} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}15}}{{\color{red}20}}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

$$
\frac{3\times 10}{1\times 10}=\frac{30}{10}
$$

$$

![](images/65/6591fd004ba2b74c2651182ce0c70302ac789d868389d057a502b8e98ac61fab.png)

We write

$$
\overrightarrow{AB}=-\overrightarrow{BA}.
$$

To compute the sum of two opposite vectors,

$$
\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BA},
$$

we can use the triangle law of addition.

According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant is the vector that goes from the tail of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ to the head of $\overrightarrow{BA}.$ Therefore, we obtain a new vector for which the tail and head are the same point, $A.$ We denote that vector as

$$
\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BA} = \overrightarrow{AA}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

The vector $\mathbf{0}$ is called the **zero vector**. The zero vector has no direction and zero magnitude. With the zero vector, the head coincides with the tail." :tutorial/id #uuid "ff30d4cd-a46e-5658-aada-2885298012f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2903 :tutorial/title "Opposite Vectors and the Zero Vector"} :step/id #uuid "9589b39e-7e79-59cb-a04d-4c80d504257a" :step/math-academy-id 15691 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097472}} {:db/id 17592186097475 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096646 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096443 :question/id #uuid "77d2bd5d-5f79-5204-8c65-395ef6414225" :question/math-academy-id "e-4276"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e9ae0161-d016-5aef-8c11-020047c66bbd" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096993} {:db/id 17592186097337} {:db/id 17592186510440} {:db/id 17592186510459}] :knowledge-point/title "Adding More Than Two Vectors Using the Triangle Law"} :step/id #uuid "79ccec21-3796-56f3-a7d4-24bb46c252eb" :step/math-academy-id 15693} {:db/id 17592186097489 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096654 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096453 :question/id #uuid "5fade14b-9fa1-5777-afe3-c061907218f6" :question/math-academy-id "e-4359"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "711d0e70-a248-5f93-a836-43bed5435d4f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096992} {:db/id 17592186097153} {:db/id 17592186510404} {:db/id 17592186510437}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting Two Vectors Using the Triangle Law"} :step/id #uuid "9525b995-7556-5826-b108-58b033c286e1" :step/math-academy-id 16022 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097475}} {:db/id 17592186097490 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097838 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to use the triangle law to add two vectors. For example, suppose that, due to overfishing, a fish population decays exponentially. The population $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = 5\,000 \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^t,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began. What can we deduce about the population of fish from this model?

The first thing to notice is that the function above is an exponential decay function of the form

$$
y(t) = a \cdot b^t.
$$

So, we can deduce the following:

- $a=5\,000$ represents the initial value. So this tells us that there were $5\,000$ fish when the overfishing began.

- $b = \dfrac 1 2$ is the decay factor. Since $0 < b < 1,$ this tells us that we're dealing with exponential decay, *not* exponential growth (for exponential growth we need $b > 1$).

- $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began." :tutorial/id #uuid "adec391e-8573-55bf-b53b-d5d15177f633" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1970 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$
m(2)-m(3).
$$

The mass of the meteor after $t=2$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}m(2) & =20\cdot (0.4)^{2} \\  & =20\cdot 0.16 \\  & =3.2.\end{aligned}
$$

The mass of the meteor after $t=3$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}m(3) & =20\cdot (0.4)^{3} \\  & =20\cdot 0.064 \\  & =1.28.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

the function's graph. For that reason, it's often helpful to plot the function when determining its range.

For example, consider the linear function 

$$
f(x) =3-2x,
$$

where $x$ is any real number. What is the range of $f(x)$?

Since this is a linear function, we only need two points to plot it. For example:

- When $x=0,$ we have $y=3.$ This gives the point $(0,3).$

- When $x=1,$ we have $y=1.$ This gives the point $(1,1).$

Plotting these two points and connecting them, we obtain the following diagram.

![](images/51/5124e487118191ae40248d4488450d065fe71712f709ac62321d749ac17b0127.png)

Notice that the graph $y=f(x)$ will cover all possible $y$-values, so the range of the function is

$$
-\infty <          y <          \infty.
$$

Using interval notation, we can also write the range as $(-\infty, \infty).$

Let's now look at an example of a linear function with a restricted domain." :tutorial/id #uuid "0a33428f-024c-5783-b5d1-b4b0f342d4a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8800 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} $$
4 \le x + 2 \le 8.
$$

To solve the compound inequality, we apply the usual operations to the middle of the inequality to isolate $x.$ Keep in mind that whatever we do to the middle, we also need to do to *both* the left-hand *and* right-hand sides.

Here, we can isolate $x$ by subtracting $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	4 & \le x + 2 \le 8 \[5pt]
	4 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} &\le x + 2 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \le 8 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \[5pt]
	2 &\le x \le 6
}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $2 \le x \le 6.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6d8fae47-5e67-5793-a585-d3781d5c4555" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8677 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid Here, we can isolate $x$ by subtracting $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	4 & \le x + 2 \le 8 \[5pt]
	4 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} &\le x + 2 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \le 8 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \[5pt]
	2 &\le x \le 6

$$
\eqalign{
	4 & \le x + 2 \le 8 \[5pt]
	4 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} &\le x + 2 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \le 8 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \[5pt]
	2 &\le x \le 6
}
$$

First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & \le -2x+3\le 5 \\ -5-3 & \le -2x+3-3\le 5-3 \\ -8 & \le -2x\le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-2.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & \le -2x\le 2 \\ \frac{-8}{-2} & \ge \frac{-2x}{-2}\ge \frac{2}{-2} \\ \frac{8}{2} & \ge x\ge -\frac{2}{2} \\ 4 & \ge x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution can be written as $4\ge x\ge -1$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
-1\le x\le 4
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{x} & =\frac{3}{5} \\ 5\cdot 2 & =3\cdot x \\ 10 & =3x \\ \frac{10}{3} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

However, there is also another method that we can use, known as the **flip method,** which involves taking the reciprocal of both sides of an equation. So, when an equation involves two fractions, we can "flip" them as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

The flip method is useful because it allows us to remove a variable from a denominator. For example, applying the flip method, we have

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}x}=\dfrac{\color{blue}3}{\color{red}5}  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\color{blue}x}{\color{red}2} = \dfrac{\color{red}5}{\color{blue}3}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & =2\cdot \frac{5}{3} \\ \cancel{2}\cdot \frac{x}{\cancel{2}} & =2\cdot \frac{5}{3} \\ x & =\frac{10}{3}\end{aligned}

is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1?$" :question/worked-solution "The full expression describing all points on our elliptic cylinder is

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1, \qquad z=k
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{R}$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1\right\}
$$

which can be written as

$$
\left\{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \dfrac{x^2}{3^2} + \dfrac{(y+1)^2}{1^2} = 1\right\}.
$$

This is an ellipse centered at $(0,-1)$ with semi-axes of lengths $3$ and $1.$"} {:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id 17592186048866} {:db/id 17592186049118} {:db/id 17592186049477} {:db/id 17592186049699} {:db/id 17592186124828 :question/id #uuid "9d23f0c9-2a90-5ec1-8032-cee754302a30" :question/math-academy-id "q-164350" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "22a180bc-4ecc-573a-b333-06c7019b8383" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola centered at $(-1,4)$" :db/id 17592186281994} {:answer/id #uuid "550bfaec-6a11-5ddf-b1d5-67ca92888f0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}^{2}" :db/id 17592186282411} {:answer/id #uuid "96935a61-eb89-5cc2-aba4-b8ddd8b9b387" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola centered at $(1,-4)$" :db/id 17592186282993} {:answer/id #uuid "d95e04a0-a388-5b35-98e8-1dca8adf8519" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A parabola centered at $(1,-4)$" :db/id 17592186283582} {:answer/id #uuid "26aa670d-074c-57a3-89ad-75bfb2454f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }x\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186519054}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186281994} :answer-field/id #uuid "bd914ec5-f35f-57ed-80b7-7031ea7255e0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284273}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1?$" :question/worked-solution "The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1\}.
$$

This is a hyperbola centered at $(-1,4).$"} {:db/id 17592186124892 :question/id #uuid "cc8b2a71-605f-561b-af0c-35843cefcc96" :question/math-academy-id "q-35569" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id $$
\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1,\,z=k
$$

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1}
$$

which can be written as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{{6}^{2}}=1}.

:topic/id #uuid "2eaffcb9-29e5-5903-a02d-080ab3e7a821" :topic/math-academy-id 1895} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125830 :tutorial/content "A **cylinder** is a surface made by the set of lines that pass through a plane curve $C$ in the $xy$-plane and are perpendicular to this plane. The curve $C$ is called the **base curve**.

The familiar two-dimensional conic sections (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas) can be used to describe cylinders. In this lesson, we'll explore these shapes.

An **elliptic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is an ellipse. If the ellipse lies in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of our elliptic cylinder is given by

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the semi-axes of the ellipse $C.$ In particular, if $a=b$, we get a **circular cylinder.**

**Watch out!** This may look like the equation of a regular ellipse. However, since we're now describing a surface in three-dimensional space, we assume that the $z$-coordinate is arbitrary. Thus, if we want $z$ to feature in our equations explicitly, we would write

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad z=k
$$

where $k\in \mathbb R.$ 

For example, the graph of the elliptic cylinder

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1
$$

is shown below. The center of its base ellipse $C$ is at the origin, and the **axis** of the elliptic cylinder (the line through the center of the cylinder) is the $z$-axis.

![](images/50/504e609e134654d258378226d90f5faa8b9f6d12313a4fcac4a23d0bfe6bea52.png)

Let's describe some properties of this elliptic cylinder:

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1,
$$

which is the base ellipse $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0)$ with semi-major and semi-minor axes of lengths $2$ and $1,$ respectively.

![](images/d0/d0e4c0630b0da60c4324330211ab1bf8090ebec067d9ebc2ac2a03056c500bd6.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to two lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/38/3813a5f43319056be03ddd8b3353ef3a8166b7495b32397c91066f40d0b33cd5.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to two lines in the $yz$-plane.

![](images/a0/a0d928060ad18d3ba677f5dd184777b833d3abf03226c04c21292e455bcd0518.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f8f004e2-d43f-5628-bbbe-4b3c7918a9f5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4931 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "21ce271d-74a1-526d-a3bb-1e1dc0da83ed" :step/math-academy-id 30776 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125519}} {:db/id 17592186125518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124587 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124398 :question/id #uuid "0cb849bd-8a9f-5305-b086-62da1a10e54f" :question/math-academy-id "e-8226"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "36c5224a-eccc-5ea9-8719-2b0dc2ddb44d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id 17592186048866} {:db/id 17592186049118} {:db/id 17592186049477} {:db/id 17592186049699}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124828} {:db/id 17592186124892} {:db/id 17592186284487} {:db/id 17592186284488} {:db/id 17592186284489} {:db/id 17592186381313} {:db/id 17592186381320} {:db/id 17592186401488} {:db/id 17592186401495} {:db/id 17592186410158} {:db/id 17592186476898} {:db/id 17592186508918}] :knowledge-point/title "The Domain of a Cylinder"} :step/id #uuid "6b214232-840a-58b5-8946-bbbc69c878d7" :step/math-academy-id 30778 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125644}} {:db/id 17592186125519 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125831 :tutorial/content "A **parabolic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is a parabola.

If the parabola $C$ opens upward or downward when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by

$$
(x-x_0)^2 = 4p(y-y_0),
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

For example, the graph of the parabolic cylinder

$$
x^2 = y
$$

is shown below. Its base curve is an upward-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The **axis** of the cylinder is the $z$-axis.

![](images/03/03ab0a28802900d8076fdd5f555bdad6582c449441c46f1de74260013cc55119.png)

The trace of this parabolic cylinder can be either a parabola or a set of lines.

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
x^2 = y,
$$

which corresponds to the base parabola $C$ with its vertex at the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/98/98124890d921c73d0cda54428ac803221d5f393384e14db2909b0138fda0fb93.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to a line in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2} & =y \\ y & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to a line in the $yz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

On the other hand, if the base parabola $C$ is left-opening or right-opening when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by

$$
(y-y_0)^2 = 4p(x-x_0),
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

For example, the graph of the parabolic cylinder

$$
y^2 = x
$$

is shown below. Its base curve is a right-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

  

![](images/a8/a87267dbd77b1561c047c6228ba0c70b08e5a48228d7e0b6a161463045d5e22b.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4026d216-b14f-558d-a7a4-cf39aa550b45" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4932 :tutorial/title "Parabolic Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "0e4c9032-faa3-5e93-a91c-a0a7db82838a" :step/math-academy-id 30779 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125526}} {:db/id 17592186125520 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124588 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124399 :question/id #uuid "64fc4653-a2ba-5013-8c70-1f4f14e5f8be" :question/math-academy-id "e-8227"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abbeda26-2fc0-5195-be26-ae79c72fc7bf" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124878} {:db/id 17592186124879} {:db/id 17592186284480} {:db/id 17592186284481} {:db/id 17592186284484} {:db/id 17592186284485} {:db/id 17592186284486} {:db/id 17592186398597} {:db/id 17592186401467} {:db/id 17592186401474} {:db/id 17592186508975}] :knowledge-point/title "Traces of Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "595c41f8-1c2f-5e89-b663-e36a44f691ac" :step/math-academy-id 30781} {:db/id 17592186125526 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125834 :tutorial/content "A **hyperbolic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is a hyperbola.

If the hyperbola $C$ is horizontal in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the hyperbolic cylinder is given by

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

 For example, the graph of the hyperbola cylinder

$$
x^2 - y^2 = 1
$$

is shown below. Its base curve is a horizontal hyperbola in the $xy$-plane centered at the origin. The **axis** of the cylinder is the $z$-axis.

![](images/e3/e3c921cc7d6a1edbb182ecf158d7b84eb0d203fd20924d07cf57ca8f8ffdc107.png)

The trace of this surface can be either a hyperbola, a set of lines, or the empty set.

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
x^2 - y^2 = 1,
$$

which is the base hyperbola $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/19/19e02f27f625dd75d12333de3b82a7a012e4f6370c729eef5cd38a633c2c8689.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to a pair of lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/56/5679b53433493d8b6e92d5aa5273be30bbf67a9db51993a925423d8514571f05.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is the empty set.

On the other hand, if the base hyperbola $C$ is vertical when viewed from the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the hyperbolic cylinder is given by

$$
\dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} = 1,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

For example, the graph of the hyperbola cylinder

$$
y^2 - x^2 = 1
$$

is shown below. Its base curve is a vertical hyperbola in the $xy$-plane centered at the origin, and the cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

  

![](images/d6/d690bca9515389bb403d0f205861af3294bc3a961df6691a5adb86de01421cff.png)

Note that for all of the cylinders discussed so far, the *domain* of each cylinder in the $xy$-plane is simply the base curve $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7260540c-2b7c-555f-9aa0-6f3dd490079b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4939 :tutorial/title "Hyperbolic Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "3f461a0c-aa8c-58dd-b9c4-e57ae5d51a3b" :step/math-academy-id 30810 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125518}} {:db/id 17592186125644 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125884 :tutorial/content "So far, we've encountered cylinders whose axes are parallel to the $z$-axis. However, we can also define cylinders whose axes are parallel to the $x$- or $y$-axes. To do this, we simply need to describe a base curve in either the $yz$-plane or the $xz$-plane. 

For an elliptic cylinder whose base ellipse $C$ is centered at the origin, the other two cases are as follows:

- Consider the elliptic cylinder $C$ whose base curve lies in the $xz$-plane.

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1
$$

In this case, the axis of the elliptic cylinder is the $y$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/f3/f32db327a6e1f54d5b346af4ea2f9b0bcfce7f82c1b6e44375f398705acd4f63.png)

- Consider the elliptic cylinder $C$ whose base curve lies in the $yz$-plane.

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1
$$

In this case, the axis of the elliptic cylinder is the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/53/5395c07f7646db4d4091e4bf176ae8d13c9c6753c322b8325dee2542480efdd4.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "12af86a6-3212-596e-a78e-92fb9ba06344" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7851 :tutorial/title "Elliptic Cylinders With Alternative Central Axes"} :step/id #uuid "2800e74a-ab30-5499-809e-31fb6deb9785" :step/math-academy-id 45321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125646}} {:db/id 17592186125646 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125886 :tutorial/content "For a parabolic cylinder whose base parabola $C$ has its vertex at the origin, the other four cases are as follows:

- When $C$ is in the $xz$-plane and $p>0,$ the axis is the $y$-axis.

![](images/79/79d1fdd86e7f615597125f5ac43e55ecd59bc298387575707348784d2d48acd0.png)

Note that if $p < 0,$ we get a reflection in the $xy$-plane or $yz$-plane of the parabolic cylinders shown above.

- When $C$ is in the $yz$-plane and $p>0,$ the axis is the $x$-axis.

![](images/73/730dccdd02e06d5f2de834f7b42c9121246aacda7595d2c5f760ae2f4c3bb5c9.png)

Note that if $p<0,$ we get a reflection in the $xy$-plane or $xz$-plane of the parabolic cylinders shown above." :tutorial/id #uuid "049a63bf-b3e2-52e8-80c1-82042790f8f2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7855 :tutorial/title "Parabolic Cylinders With Alternative Central Axes"} :step/id #uuid "8fa4a35a-4cb0-5fd5-99f4-903b12b2986b" :step/math-academy-id 45325 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125647}} {:db/id 17592186125647 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125887 :tutorial/content "For a hyperbolic cylinder whose base hyperbola $C$ has its vertex at the origin, the other four cases are as follows:

- When $C$ is in the $xz$-plane, the axis of the hyperbolic cylinder is the $y$-axis.

![](images/28/28f79c28aa6dfaa28b7b8ddd6d196bcb21db18411454c655a3365be52e8c6bc7.png)

- When $C$ is in the $yz$-plane, the axis of the hyperbolic cylinder is the $x$-axis.

The curve $C$ is called the **base curve**.

The familiar two-dimensional conic sections (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas) can be used to describe cylinders. In this lesson, we'll explore these shapes.

An **elliptic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is an ellipse. If the ellipse lies in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of our elliptic cylinder is given by

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the semi-axes of the ellipse $C.$ In particular, if $a=b$, we get a **circular cylinder.**

**Watch out!** This may look like the equation of a regular ellipse. However, since we're now describing a surface in three-dimensional space, we assume that the $z$-coordinate is arbitrary. Thus, if we want $z$ to feature in our equations explicitly, we would write

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad z=k
$$

where $k\in \mathbb R.$ 

For example, the graph of the elliptic cylinder

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1
$$

is shown below. The center of its base ellipse $C$ is at the origin, and the **axis** of the elliptic cylinder (the line through the center of the cylinder) is the $z$-axis.

![](images/50/504e609e134654d258378226d90f5faa8b9f6d12313a4fcac4a23d0bfe6bea52.png)

Let's describe some properties of this elliptic cylinder:

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1,
$$

which is the base ellipse $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0)$ with semi-major and semi-minor axes of lengths $2$ and $1,$ respectively.

![](images/d0/d0e4c0630b0da60c4324330211ab1bf8090ebec067d9ebc2ac2a03056c500bd6.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to two lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/38/3813a5f43319056be03ddd8b3353ef3a8166b7495b32397c91066f40d0b33cd5.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to two lines in the $yz$-plane.

$$

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

On the other hand, if the base parabola $C$ is left-opening or right-opening when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by

$$
(y-y_0)^2 = 4p(x-x_0),
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

For example, the graph of the parabolic cylinder

$$

$$

is shown below. Its base curve is a right-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

![](images/53/5395c07f7646db4d4091e4bf176ae8d13c9c6753c322b8325dee2542480efdd4.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "12af86a6-3212-596e-a78e-92fb9ba06344" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7851 :tutorial/title "Elliptic Cylinders With Alternative Central Axes"} :step/id #uuid "2800e74a-ab30-5499-809e-31fb6deb9785" :step/math-academy-id 45321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125646}} {:db/id 17592186125831 :tutorial/content "A **parabolic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is a parabola.

If the parabola $C$ opens upward or downward when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by

$$
(x-x_0)^2 = 4p(y-y_0),
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

$$
x^2 = y
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
x^2 = y,
$$

which corresponds to the base parabola $C$ with its vertex at the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/98/98124890d921c73d0cda54428ac803221d5f393384e14db2909b0138fda0fb93.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to a line in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2} & =y \\ y & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to a line in the $yz$-plane.

![](images/f8/f87dbd180911db28a515dfe11da99d5d9d06da74e7ef117ea0a6df88018e95a2.png)

On the other hand, if the base parabola $C$ is left-opening or right-opening when viewed from the $xy$-plane and its vertex is at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the parabolic cylinder is given by

$$
(y-y_0)^2 = 4p(x-x_0),
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

$$

is shown below. Its base curve is a right-opening parabola in the $xy$-plane with its vertex at the origin. The cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

  

![](images/a8/a87267dbd77b1561c047c6228ba0c70b08e5a48228d7e0b6a161463045d5e22b.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4026d216-b14f-558d-a7a4-cf39aa550b45" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4932 :tutorial/title "Parabolic Cylinders"} {:db/id 17592186125526 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125834 :tutorial/content "A **hyperbolic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is a hyperbola.

If the hyperbola $C$ is horizontal in the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the hyperbolic cylinder is given by

$$
\dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

 For example, the graph of the hyperbola cylinder

$$
x^2 - y^2 = 1
$$

is shown below. Its base curve is a horizontal hyperbola in the $xy$-plane centered at the origin. The **axis** of the cylinder is the $z$-axis.

![](images/e3/e3c921cc7d6a1edbb182ecf158d7b84eb0d203fd20924d07cf57ca8f8ffdc107.png)

The trace of this surface can be either a hyperbola, a set of lines, or the empty set.

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
x^2 - y^2 = 1,
$$

which is the base hyperbola $C$ centered at the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/19/19e02f27f625dd75d12333de3b82a7a012e4f6370c729eef5cd38a633c2c8689.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to a pair of lines in the $xz$-plane.

![](images/56/5679b53433493d8b6e92d5aa5273be30bbf67a9db51993a925423d8514571f05.png)

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is the empty set.

On the other hand, if the base hyperbola $C$ is vertical when viewed from the $xy$-plane and is centered at $(x_0,y_0,0)$, then the equation of the hyperbolic cylinder is given by

$$
\dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} = 1,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

For example, the graph of the hyperbola cylinder

$$
y^2 - x^2 = 1
$$

is shown below. Its base curve is a vertical hyperbola in the $xy$-plane centered at the origin, and the cylinder's axis is the $z$-axis.

  

![](images/d6/d690bca9515389bb403d0f205861af3294bc3a961df6691a5adb86de01421cff.png)

Note that for all of the cylinders discussed so far, the *domain* of each cylinder in the $xy$-plane is simply the base curve $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7260540c-2b7c-555f-9aa0-6f3dd490079b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4939 :tutorial/title "Hyperbolic Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "3f461a0c-aa8c-58dd-b9c4-e57ae5d51a3b" :step/math-academy-id 30810 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125518}} {:db/id 17592186125520 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124588 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124399 :question/id #uuid "64fc4653-a2ba-5013-8c70-1f4f14e5f8be" :question/math-academy-id "e-8227"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abbeda26-2fc0-5195-be26-ae79c72fc7bf" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124878} {:db/id 17592186124879} {:db/id 17592186284480} {:db/id 17592186284481} {:db/id 17592186284484} {:db/id 17592186284485} {:db/id 17592186284486} {:db/id 17592186398597} {:db/id 17592186401467} {:db/id 17592186401474} {:db/id 17592186508975}] :knowledge-point/title "Traces of Cylinders"} :step/id #uuid "595c41f8-1c2f-5e89-b663-e36a44f691ac" :step/math-academy-id 30781} {:db/id 17592186125834 :tutorial/content "A **hyperbolic cylinder** is a cylinder whose base curve $C$ is a hyperbola.

$\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1?$" :question/worked-solution "The full expression describing all points on our elliptic cylinder is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1}
$$

which can be written as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1}.
$$

$$
\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1}

which can be written as

$$

$$
\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1\}.
$$

$$
\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{P(x)}\right)  = 0.
$$

This is because as $x$ increases, any polynomial $P(x)$ will grow without bound, and therefore its reciprocal shrinks to zero.

$$
\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{x^3 - x^2 + 1}\right)  = 0.
$$

Likewise, the expression $(2x-5)^4$ can be multiplied out to become a non-constant polynomial, so we have

$$
\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{ (2x-5)^4 }\right)  = 0.

![](images/ea/ea736c37f855415e54d8b3a3775fab07159b5de4a368bee45bba13ae261372da.png)

We see that the curve approaches zero as $x$ approaches positive infinity. The same is true as $x$ approaches negative infinity. So, we write 

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=0.
$$

The same is true for $\dfrac{1}{x^n}$ where $n$ is *any* positive integer. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=0\, & \text{and}\,{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=0 \\ {lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})=0\, & \text{and}\,{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})=0 \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

and so on. This is because as the size of $x$ increases, the size of $\dfrac{1}{x^n}$ decreases." :tutorial/id #uuid "cc60ef45-0775-563f-b940-b75c2072bb10" :tutorial/math-academy-id 198 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "18483bb1-f2e9-5d0c-9086-c24211966036" :step/math-academy-id 366 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125493}} {:db/id 17592186125585 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125720 :tutorial/content "Let's again look at the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}.$

![](images/e8/e8b24529b70e32a32eb45fc9ce5d907ca74020a940b46fbf63b5386bf2d8cd9d.png)

From the graph, we see that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0^-} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = -\infty \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0^+} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \infty.
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not the same, we conclude that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \textrm{DNE}.
$$

Any function of the form $y = \dfrac{1}{x^n},$ where $n$ is an *odd* natural number, has the same shape as $y = \dfrac{1}{x},$ and consequently the limit behavior is the same.  For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})=-\infty , & \,{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})=\infty , \\ {lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})=-\infty , & \,{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})=\infty , \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

and so on. For all of the above, the limit of the function does not exist at $x=0$ because the left and right limits are not the same." :tutorial/id #uuid "c947a280-46a8-5dc9-ba95-a6a2486bc4e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 200 :tutorial/title "Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Odd Power"} :step/id #uuid "c7a8cf4a-7017-5fdf-b283-ad717892866d" :step/math-academy-id 369 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125586}} {:db/id 17592186125586 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124626 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124286 :question/id #uuid "1fd5312f-c992-5218-bcfd-9bc235e9cd53" :question/math-academy-id "e-41"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f015a46e-7493-558d-a1d8-c2d90f9306ab" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186051049}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124986} {:db/id 17592186125145} {:db/id 17592186233861} {:db/id 17592186234509} {:db/id 17592186234510} {:db/id 17592186565415} {:db/id 17592186565476}] :knowledge-point/title "Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Odd Power"} :step/id #uuid "b51ac528-c3e2-5c7f-b774-1a784b67608a" :step/math-academy-id 370 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125587}} {:db/id 17592186125587 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125721 :tutorial/content "Now let's look at the graph of $y = \dfrac{1}{x^2}.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-3}}+9{x}^{2}.

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = f'(g(a)) \cdot g'(a)
$$

Let $f$ and $g$ be functions such that

- $g$ is differentiable at $a$,

- $f$ is differentiable at $g(a)$.

Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $a$, and we compute its derivative as follows.

We start with the definition of the derivative:

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a}
$$

Since $g$ is differentiable at $a$, it is also continuous there. Hence $g(x) \to g(a)$ as $x \to a$. For $x$ sufficiently close to $a$, we have $g(x) \ne g(a)$, so we may write

$$
\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a} 
= \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{g(x) - g(a)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(a)}{x - a}.
$$

Taking the limit as $x \to a$, and using the product rule for limits (which applies since both limits exist), we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘g)^{′}(a) & ={lim}_{x\to a}(\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot \frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot {lim}_{x\to a}\frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a} \\  & ={f}^{′}(g(a))\cdot {g}^{′}(a)\end{aligned}
$$

as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "d34fc877-5572-53a2-b957-2c5d44a488f3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13330 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "9ad2def5-511c-587f-9847-fa7af8e06405" :step/math-academy-id 466057} {:db/id 17592186097783 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097872 :tutorial/content "The **chain rule** for differentiation states that the derivative of a composite function $f(g(x))$ is given by

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

There is some intuition behind this rule: if we think of the derivatives as fractions, the ${\textrm{d}g}$'s would appear to cancel out.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\cancel{\text{d}g}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{d}g}}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

To see how the chain rule can be used to differentiate a function like 

$$
f(x) = (1+2x)^3,
$$

first, notice that the function can be written as a composite function

$$
f(g) = g^3, \qquad g(x) = 1+2x.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}g}({g}^{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+2x) \\  & =3{g}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =6{g}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(x) = 1+2x$ for $g,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =6(1+2x)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We'll provide a derivation of the chain rule at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "743ad997-8732-5c0f-9676-ff1d44f3b513" :tutorial/math-academy-id 415 :tutorial/title {{field-1}}
$)$" :question/worked-solution "Let $g(x)={x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}$ and $f(g(x))=g(x)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{2})^{′}=2g, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{4}-3{x}^{3})^{′}=4{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =2g\cdot (4{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}) \\  & =2({x}^{4}-3{x}^{3})(\,4{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}\,).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "35b3efb8-a2d4-59c0-b538-ee4b244189e0"} {:db/id 17592186520543 :step/content {:db/id 17592186520473 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bf96aed-c4c2-50a0-9312-269557ced95f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8(1-3x)^{7}" :db/id 17592186520029} {:answer/id #uuid "4793072d-d61e-5f93-bb0c-993627ee72c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-24(1+3x)^{7}" :db/id 17592186520100} {:answer/id #uuid "99709777-eb56-5d41-ac58-1c43410ac856" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-24(1-3x)^{7}" :db/id 17592186520209} {:answer/id #uuid "d2298536-2087-59b8-a435-384b956031dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24(1+3x)^{7}" :db/id 17592186520286} {:answer/id #uuid "e7514498-fddf-54d8-9478-ff10ceb72766" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3(1-3x)^{7}" :db/id 17592186520330}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520209} :answer-field/id #uuid "44da7608-9cb4-57b2-9694-53ee352f7833" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186520387}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "73597027-954f-5bff-8c64-de058a3fe822" :question/math-academy-id "q-107296" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)={(1-3x)}^{8},$ find ${f}^{′}(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $g(x)=1-3x$ and $f(g(x))=g(x)^{8}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{8})^{′}=8{g}^{7}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(1-3x)^{′}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =8{g}^{7}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-24(1-3x)^{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4350c72e-f9bd-5210-90fd-d37e9cc293c0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520579}} {:db/id 17592186520551 :step/content {:db/id 17592186520516 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33c7c493-bcdb-5703-aa16-7951eec23ed2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186520068}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520068} :answer-field/id #uuid "3b694189-fec1-5a06-8456-a524e215acf6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186520382}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fa666076-05a3-50c7-be3d-b7a39d6d4f55" :question/math-academy-id "q-314192" :question/problem "The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{4x+1}$ at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "51f59503-df73-54cc-af64-3dcb163fe7d6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520538}} {:db/id 17592186520579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186520487 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "454a250f-2e0e-5eff-ad08-2e1a4569c3b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520091} {:answer/id #uuid "4cf36f6a-ac30-5d76-9499-88f79530ef58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520108} {:answer/id #uuid "a63c2527-a87a-5317-bb52-435b49980a68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520218} {:answer/id #uuid "ceae46e6-5020-51b1-a35e-422b64ddda99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520281} {:answer/id #uuid "edcc6c31-a212-5340-8bdb-e1b0f8c22746" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520341}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520091} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e463a5a-0bf7-5c15-8a84-e8fb513aab4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186520404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "98cde390-f268-5ffd-9f2f-31f016a0c432" :question/math-academy-id "q-107303" :question/problem "Given that $y=\sqrt{2x-1},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2x-1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}.\end{aligned}

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-{x}^{2}+2x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-2x+2) \\  & =\frac{-2x+2}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{-2x+2}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{-2(1)+2}{2\sqrt{-{1}^{2}+2(1)}} \\  & =\frac{0}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "dd09ffd1-587d-547b-937b-c610cc67ad37" :step/next {:db/id 17592186542241}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "496974f1-cd7b-5abe-b03b-8caf3c2ef7ba" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
