$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+z)) \\  & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{xy}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+z)) \\  & =2x\cdot \frac{1}{y+z} \\  & =\frac{2x}{y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xyz}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{2x}{y+z}) \\  & =2x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{y+z}) \\  & =2x\cdot (-\frac{1}{(y+z)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{(y+z)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{xyz}(x,y,z)$ at $(-5,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(-5,2,3) & =-\frac{2(-5)}{(2+3)^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268923 :question/id #uuid "01b2f238-4be0-502a-a439-500d85cd72b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-132961" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00508df2-67fc-5789-9478-c3e2d42771e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186266152} {:answer/id #uuid "44da4fc7-1df8-536a-a190-f8c23a3e32f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\pi " :db/id 17592186266758} {:answer/id #uuid "63a9b984-28e7-58d3-8128-0a6d4ca98f26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186267021} {:answer/id #uuid "88f1885b-f866-5cf3-96ea-874e43e6a210" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186267363} {:answer/id #uuid "8ebfbd8f-e225-52f2-af81-73501dcd099d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186267416}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186266152} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f17d030-5507-55e9-8f15-4689404588ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268545}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Evaluate ${f}_{xxz}(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi )$ for $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡xyz) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\cdot yz \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{x}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\cdot (-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\cdot (2z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}z(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xyz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz))\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ at $(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ) & =-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot \pi \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )+1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268924 :question/id #uuid "5eef046b-e675-5de1-b784-361653847836" :question/math-academy-id "q-132984"} {:db/id 17592186335787 :question/id #uuid "101d6e00-46ae-511e-8fb6-40ece63bbd97" :question/math-academy-id "q-65068" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124442 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83724b66-0f15-5b94-9576-76e9dfd56d38" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Higher-Order Derivatives"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "35449759-c15b-512f-8420-1fb63ecd365b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2(1+xy){e}^{xy}" :db/id 17592186333479} {:answer/id #uuid "6ee18fc9-cbc6-586c-bc71-475637c324b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(2-xy){e}^{xy}" :db/id 17592186333998} {:answer/id #uuid "9a0371f6-0b4a-5973-b88a-0f71945345be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(1+xy){e}^{xy}" :db/id 17592186334348} {:answer/id #uuid "c8509045-b540-5b6c-809d-592048041afb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x(2-xy){e}^{xy}" :db/id 17592186334732} {:answer/id #uuid "e331b700-4987-5e42-86ca-0e1830625b2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y(2+xy){e}^{xy}" :db/id 17592186334967}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e331b700-4987-5e42-86ca-0e1830625b2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y(2+xy){e}^{xy}" :db/id 17592186334967} :answer-field/id #uuid "8f091079-d683-5612-93c2-5fcf60f69e17" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186335512}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Calculate ${f}_{xxy}(x,y)$ given that $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}) \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy}) \\  & =y(y{e}^{xy}) \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${f}_{xxy}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xx}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{xx}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{xy}) \\  & =2y\cdot {e}^{xy}+{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot x \\  & =y(2+xy){e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335788 :question/id #uuid "ab0f3803-2840-52ec-8174-767389c2fcc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-65071" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0548138d-e543-5a54-a872-c6505ae35f31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186333031} {:answer/id #uuid "3dd21545-2656-5f34-8899-9e63ce0f1a99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2y}{x}" :db/id 17592186333573} {:answer/id #uuid "56f12986-c08d-5855-9c32-e38ca3128af3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186333777} {:answer/id #uuid "7279d9a1-e1cd-5962-b045-74040fa8edd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y}{4x}" :db/id 17592186334026} {:answer/id #uuid "810185ca-f52f-5e5b-a85b-df54ad11e6a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{4+y}{x}" :db/id 17592186334135}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333031} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7a6c17f-ff74-5dd2-941a-c73839c7e4a2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Calculate ${f}_{yxx}(x,y)$ given that $f(x,y)={y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =2y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})) \\  & =2y\cdot \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${f}_{yxx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{yx}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4y}{x}) \\  & =\frac{0\cdot x-4y\cdot 1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348393 :question/id #uuid "09777d76-95e6-5bbb-83f0-f307b490599a" :question/math-academy-id "q-80474"} {:db/id 17592186381062 :question/id #uuid "a11d21f8-cefe-5922-beca-1c00b4452f90" :question/math-academy-id "q-132972" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124442 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83724b66-0f15-5b94-9576-76e9dfd56d38" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Higher-Order Derivatives"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8654559e-0c2f-5da0-a22d-c4d32b252a1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186381064} {:answer/id #uuid "01d037ce-31b1-550d-9f64-39f98a921a6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186381065} {:answer/id #uuid "3a7e3c17-36aa-5bbb-a443-d147a29832c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186381066} {:answer/id #uuid "4d77f975-e483-5da8-a655-8c2d4d00e88f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186381067} {:answer/id #uuid "8a0eeeeb-b267-56a5-bb8c-8f5ff5f66c9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186381068}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "8654559e-0c2f-5da0-a22d-c4d32b252a1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186381064} :answer-field/id #uuid "863a0f4c-944c-569a-949c-d1714005af42" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186381063}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate ${f}_{zyx}(2,4,-2)$ for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{3}\sqrt{y}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{z}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}{z}^{3}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zy}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{z}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =\frac{3x{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ at $(2,4,-2):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(2,4,-2) & =\frac{3(2)(-2)^{2}}{\sqrt{4}}=\frac{24}{2}=12\end{aligned}

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =xy\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =\frac{xy}{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)\cdot (x+y+z)^{2}-({x}^{2}+xz)\cdot (2(x+y+z)\cdot 1)}{(x+y+z)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)(x+y+z)-2({x}^{2}+xz)}{(x+y+z)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

17592186125269 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125724 :tutorial/content "Just like we can compute second derivatives of single-variable functions, we can also compute second derivatives of multivariable functions.

For example, consider the two-variable function

$$
f (x, y)= x y^2 + e^{xy}.
$$

Its two first-order partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={y}^{2}+y{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =2xy+x{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_x(x,y)$ and $f_y(x,y)$ are themselves functions that are differentiable with respect to both $x$ and $y,$ we can compute the **second-order partial derivatives** as well. 

- The partial derivatives of $f_x(x,y)$ with respect to $x$ and $y,$ denoted $f_{xx}$ and $f_{xy}$ respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{x}(x,y))={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y))=2y+xy{e}^{xy}+{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The partial derivatives of $f_y(x,y)$ with respect to $x$ and $y,$ denoted $f_{yx}$ and $f_{yy}$ respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y))=2y+xy{e}^{xy}+{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{y}(x,y))=2x+{x}^{2}{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

The partial derivatives $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$ are called **mixed partial derivatives** because they involve taking the partial derivatives with respect to different variables, $x$ and $y.$

The following alternative notations are also widely used to represent second-order partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{x}^{2}}(f) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}={f}_{xx}\,\,\,\,\,\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{y}^{2}}(f)=\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}={f}_{yy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂y\,∂x}(f) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y\,∂x}={f}_{xy}\,\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x\,∂y}(f)=\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x\,∂y}={f}_{yx}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** In our example, the two mixed partial derivatives were equal:

$$
f_{xy}(x,y) = 2y + xye^{xy} + e^{xy} = f_{yx}(x,y)
$$

Later, we will see that under rather mild conditions on $f,$ we almost always have that $f_{xy}=f_{yx}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "feb54aa0-17fb-5468-8b99-14174a6bd059" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2397 17592186125272 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125725 :tutorial/content "We can also define other **higher order partial derivatives** such as $f_{xxy}, \, f_{xxyy}, \, f_{xyxy},$ etc. 

For instance, the function $f(x,y,z)= z\cos(xy)$ has the first-order partial derivative

$$
f_y(x,y,z) = -xz \sin(xy)
$$

and the second-order partial derivative

$$
f_{yx}(x,y,z)= -x yz \cos{\left(x y \right)} - z\sin{\left(x y \right)}.
$$

If we differentiate again, with respect to $x,$ then we get the **third-order partial derivative** $f_{yxx}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{yx}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-xyz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =-yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xyz(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y)-z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\cdot y \\  & =x{y}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

In general, to compute a $n$th-order partial derivative, we need to compute a sequence of $n$ individual derivatives." :tutorial/id #uuid "e256986d-ca95-50b3-a16c-0f46005b5c66" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2398 :tutorial/title "Higher-Order Partial Derivatives for Functions of  More Than Two Variables"} :step/id #uuid "f8b4cf47-e81c-516c-8eef-7d544743362a" :step/math-academy-id 10566 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125273}} {:db/id 17592186125273 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124442 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124246 :question/id #uuid "a41bfb06-4372-5124-b910-4b35f19d148b" :question/math-academy-id "e-3130"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83724b66-0f15-5b94-9576-76e9dfd56d38" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124939} {:db/id 17592186124948} {:db/id 17592186268922} {:db/id 17592186268923} {:db/id 17592186268924} {:db/id 17592186335787} {:db/id 17592186335788} {:db/id 17592186348393} {:db/id 17592186381062} {:db/id 17592186381069} {:db/id 17592186382131} {:db/id 17592186422010} {:db/id 17592186422011} {:db/id 17592186436906} {:db/id 17592186436909} {:db/id 17592186483391}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Higher-Order Derivatives"} :step/id #uuid "25a77626-7a96-5d1b-b087-a01012cbeb91" :step/math-academy-id 10567}] :activity/title "Higher-Order Partial Derivatives" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124726} {:db/id 17592186125269 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125724 :tutorial/content "Just like we can compute second derivatives of single-variable functions, we can also compute second derivatives of multivariable functions.

For example, consider the two-variable function

$$
f (x, y)= x y^2 + e^{xy}.
$$

Its two first-order partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={y}^{2}+y{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =2xy+x{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_x(x,y)$ and $f_y(x,y)$ are themselves functions that are differentiable with respect to both $x$ and $y,$ we can compute the **second-order partial derivatives** as well. 

- The partial derivatives of $f_x(x,y)$ with respect to $x$ and $y,$ denoted $f_{xx}$ and $f_{xy}$ respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{x}(x,y))={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y))=2y+xy{e}^{xy}+{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The partial derivatives of $f_y(x,y)$ with respect to $x$ and $y,$ denoted $f_{yx}$ and $f_{yy}$ respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y))=2y+xy{e}^{xy}+{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{y}(x,y))=2x+{x}^{2}{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

The partial derivatives $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$ are called **mixed partial derivatives** because they involve taking the partial derivatives with respect to different variables, $x$ and $y.$

The following alternative notations are also widely used to represent second-order partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{x}^{2}}(f) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}={f}_{xx}\,\,\,\,\,\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{y}^{2}}(f)=\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}={f}_{yy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂y\,∂x}(f) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y\,∂x}={f}_{xy}\,\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x\,∂y}(f)=\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x\,∂y}={f}_{yx}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** In our example, the two mixed partial derivatives were equal:

$$
f_{xy}(x,y) = 2y + xye^{xy} + e^{xy} = f_{yx}(x,y)
$$

Later, we will see that under rather mild conditions on $f,$ we almost always have that $f_{xy}=f_{yx}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "feb54aa0-17fb-5468-8b99-14174a6bd059" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2397 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0eaae658-c43c-5756-80c4-c4462162b555" :step/math-academy-id 10558 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125270}} {:db/id 17592186125724 :tutorial/content "Just like we can compute second derivatives of single-variable functions, we can also compute second derivatives of multivariable functions.

"a25341f7-8d06-561b-9802-42d2f9c792e8" :step/math-academy-id 10563 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125272}} {:db/id 17592186125272 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125725 :tutorial/content "We can also define other **higher order partial derivatives** such as $f_{xxy}, \, f_{xxyy}, \, f_{xyxy},$ etc. 

For instance, the function $f(x,y,z)= z\cos(xy)$ has the first-order partial derivative

$$
f_y(x,y,z) = -xz \sin(xy)
$$

and the second-order partial derivative

$$
f_{yx}(x,y,z)= -x yz \cos{\left(x y \right)} - z\sin{\left(x y \right)}.
$$

If we differentiate again, with respect to $x,$ then we get the **third-order partial derivative** $f_{yxx}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{yx}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-xyz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =-yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xyz(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y)-z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\cdot y \\  & =x{y}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

In general, to compute a $n$th-order partial derivative, we need to compute a sequence of $n$ individual derivatives." :tutorial/id #uuid "e256986d-ca95-50b3-a16c-0f46005b5c66" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2398 :tutorial/title "Higher-Order Partial Derivatives for Functions of  More Than Two Variables"} :step/id #uuid "f8b4cf47-e81c-516c-8eef-7d544743362a" :step/math-academy-id 10566 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125273}} {:db/id 17592186125725 :tutorial/content "We can also define other **higher order partial derivatives** such as $f_{xxy}, \, f_{xxyy}, \, f_{xyxy},$ etc.

$$

$$

$g(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${g}_{x}(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(({x}^{2}+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${g}_{x}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${g}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({g}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${g}_{xxy}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xxy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({g}_{xx}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =4y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "25f65be6-b106-53d1-9640-27a18badcd80" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422015}} {:db/id 17592186422013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186422010 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07b7ad2e-54cc-50e3-9ca3-0b8efd17be6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4y+{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186421994} {:answer/id #uuid "1f109dc7-15d8-584f-8e2b-595762c1a061" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4xy+y{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186421996} {:answer/id #uuid "44455996-432d-5a3d-8b99-8ba088ea40bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2xy+{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186421998} {:answer/id #uuid "5e886d04-bc8d-58c5-9141-d4629aa452fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x{y}^{2}+y{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186421999} {:answer/id #uuid "e3c5be38-2517-52b4-89a2-e748dfb3f71f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y+x+{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186422007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186421994} :answer-field/id #uuid "31dfaa29-640a-5223-927a-6d7e182b7cd8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186422009}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "11508c24-c4aa-589a-b2fa-c4b12396bfe7" :question/math-academy-id "q-65070" :question/problem "Calculate ${f}_{xyx}(x,y)$ given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+y{e}^{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+y{e}^{x}) \\  & =2x\cdot {y}^{2}+y\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xy}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}+y{e}^{x}) \\  & =2x\cdot 2y+1\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & =4xy+{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${f}_{xyx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xy}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{xy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+{e}^{x}) \\  & =4\cdot 1\cdot y+{e}^{x} \\  & =4y+{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4932cd51-46e5-51d8-99f7-f0e3336e3476" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422012}} {:db/id 17592186422014 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124932 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01b1340c-9ea7-510e-a7fe-a5318d1aa165" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y" :db/id 17592186421993} {:answer/id #uuid "2ea483d9-4903-536f-a106-b11346fafb16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x\operatorname{cos}⁡y" :db/id 17592186421997} {:answer/id #uuid "646a4289-2437-5a76-800d-038e82b06562" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)" :db/id 17592186422000} {:answer/id #uuid "654452d8-a947-5e7b-b22c-8a13e2ef81d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)" :db/id 17592186422001} {:answer/id #uuid "6b0fbde1-6b7d-56c5-b32e-24ed9e9df6a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y" :db/id 17592186422002}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186421997} :answer-field/id #uuid "f436de7c-3f9a-5c8c-8ef3-8a7a55ee418d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122192}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9fe7b82e-efd4-53ad-afa8-cb700e6400e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-35936" :question/problem "Find ${f}_{xy}(x,y)+{f}_{yx}(x,y)$ given that  ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}_{xy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

To find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

first-order partial derivative ${g}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$

$$

 

To find ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({g}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we evaluate ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ and ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})=\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{6} \\ {g}_{yy}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})=-\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =xy\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =\frac{xy}{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zy}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{z}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{xy}{x+y+z}) \\  & =\frac{x\cdot (x+y+z)-xy\cdot (1)}{(x+y+z)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+xz-xy}{(x+y+z)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)\cdot (x+y+z)^{2}-({x}^{2}+xz)\cdot (2(x+y+z)\cdot 1)}{(x+y+z)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)(x+y+z)-2({x}^{2}+xz)}{(x+y+z)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ at $(1,1,-1):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(1,1,-1) & =\frac{(2(1)+(-1))(1+1+(-1))-2({1}^{2}+1(-1))}{(1+1+(-1))^{3}}=\frac{(1)(1)-2(0)}{(1)^{3}}=1\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Next, we find ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)\cdot (x+y+z)^{2}-({x}^{2}+xz)\cdot (2(x+y+z)\cdot 1)}{(x+y+z)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)(x+y+z)-2({x}^{2}+xz)}{(x+y+z)^{3}}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

 

To find ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$

$$

Finally, we have

$$
{g}_{xx}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3})-{g}_{yy}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3})=\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6})=\sqrt{3}.

:question/worked-solution "To find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})) \\  & =y\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})) \\  & =-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

To find ${f}_{yy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})-2{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y)+{f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})-2{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})-2y(y+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7500e142-5145-59e0-8086-fdd6d710a0a6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483431}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28fd9f48-019d-5f27-baf0-6a1841493cc4" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2xy}{3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}
$$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=0$
- **II.** The limit evaluates to $\frac{2}{3}$ along the path $y=x$
- **III.** The limit does not exist" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2xy}{3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}} & =\frac{2(0)(0)}{3({0}^{2})-{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0-0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=0}\,\frac{2xy}{3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2x(0)}{3({0}^{2})-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2xy}{3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x(x)}{3{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2xy}{3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265723 :question/id #uuid "7bd92abc-0899-50b8-83be-62e32b920d95" :question/math-academy-id "q-129408"} {:db/id 17592186335802 :question/id #uuid "ccd0f4b9-0dbd-51e2-a95c-14471c65ba52" :question/math-academy-id "q-65145"} {:db/id 17592186345004 :question/id #uuid "d5fe00a2-ab56-5281-b3c2-6fe8dad2417a" :question/math-academy-id "q-74964"} {:db/id 17592186345005 :question/id #uuid "56c07c72-df51-5ec4-88ac-9185b7690371" :question/math-academy-id "q-74966"} {:db/id 17592186377708 :question/id #uuid "6323a167-9fc1-5848-81f1-63d34a9c63ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-74965" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8958422f-4c02-53af-a3e5-28f8445d5bc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186377710} {:answer/id #uuid "6f7dc054-8a42-5213-b120-534bafd7ab86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186377711} {:answer/id #uuid "7ad9cc3c-2948-54af-96ab-97ac3dc5dd75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186377712} {:answer/id #uuid "de9768d4-de86-55ac-a72b-b0470b48216c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{DNE}" :db/id 17592186377713} {:answer/id #uuid "1b2466e9-2081-57a2-b9cc-0260610356d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186377714}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377713} :answer-field/id #uuid "f14349ec-0b87-5b7c-b87c-2368f3340f77" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186377709}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "${lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}

- Statement II is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-{x}^{2},$ we have

$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186508069 :question/id #uuid "6b2bedc8-52f9-5d40-afcd-8617235afd0f" :question/math-academy-id "q-129401" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15c9e982-2244-5a23-aac9-ea8f242dfd59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186507626} {:answer/id #uuid "2c45373f-5f36-5270-9c27-ce7558fa56c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186507653} {:answer/id #uuid "59f30dc1-5f5d-5fdc-a739-06dad6b23c63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186507728} {:answer/id #uuid "5beae258-194a-5396-abb9-d22777307972" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{DNE}" :db/id 17592186507731} {:answer/id #uuid "824d43de-2c6c-5256-ab7d-e1e81ca546b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186507793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507731} :answer-field/id #uuid "f962e375-138e-5ba3-a11f-61cf507ac9c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186508030}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Determine ${lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & =\frac{{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(1,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,y=0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{0}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,x=1}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}=\text{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186565425 :question/id #uuid "416deefa-43e7-520e-bca5-f8da057711d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-74967"} {:db/id 17592186565432 :question/id #uuid substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (4,4)}\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}=\frac{4-4}{\sqrt{4}-\sqrt{4}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (4,4)}\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}} & ={lim}_{x\to (4,4)}\frac{(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (4,4)}\frac{(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{(\sqrt{x})^{2}-(\sqrt{y})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (4,4)}\frac{(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (4,4)}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (4,4)}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}) & =\sqrt{4}+\sqrt{4} \\  & =2+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $4.$"} {:db/id 17592186265716 :question/id #uuid "d8bc5519-0c3a-5438-9140-d93c11fd7b22" :question/math-academy-id "q-129342" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52b2e738-d4ff-5a73-bf88-ee96a546601e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186263713} {:answer/id #uuid "6e5d18cd-26e9-513a-9ac2-d9e28cdc3a96" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186263957} {:answer/id #uuid "859fba6d-65df-52f9-8934-78218673bfa0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186264151} {:answer/id #uuid "b3999021-6e0d-58f6-8af2-534ecd301f3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186264540} {:answer/id #uuid "f16bc0b6-a366-5c5f-a505-fcaf77e8d63c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186265120}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186265120} :answer-field/id #uuid "828835a1-d776-5ae6-8933-2aafe083fed7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265474}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "${lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}=$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows:

$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2}}{x-y-2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{1+2}}{3-1-2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2}}{x-y-2} & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{2}-(\sqrt{y+2})^{2}}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{x-y-2}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$

1931} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125288 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125731 :tutorial/content "We can extend our knowledge of limits to multivariable functions. We'll first consider the two-variable case. 

We denote $\mathbf{x}=(x,y)$ and $\mathbf{x}_0 = (a,b)$ as a particular, fixed vector. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined in some neighborhood of $\mathbf x_0.$ 

Then, the notation

$$
\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{x}_0} f (x,y) = L
$$

means that the value of $f$ can be made as close as we want to $L,$ provided that $\mathbf x$ is sufficiently close to $\mathbf{x}_0.$

A few things to note:

- This definition of a limit also extends to functions of more than two variables in the natural way.

- All of the rules set out by the algebra of limits are valid for functions of several variables.

We say that $f(x,y)$ is **continuous** at $(a,b)$ if

$$
\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (a,b)} f (x,y) = f(a,b).
$$

So, if a function is continuous at $(a,b),$ then the limit can be evaluated by simply plugging $(x,y) = (a,b)$ into the function.

To demonstrate, let's calculate the following limit:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1)}} \dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2}
$$

This function is continuous for all $(x,y)$ with the exception of $(0,0)$ where the denominator vanishes. Since the point $(2,1)$ does not cause the denominator to vanish, we can calculate the limit by substituting $(x,y) = (2,1)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "eccfdda1-288a-5169-adde-a00163fa348f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2480 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a0c271d5-ca3c-5651-a78d-a2b18242c45c" :step/math-academy-id 17592186125466}} {:db/id 17592186125291 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125732 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a function of a single variable $f(x),$ if the left and right limits both exist and are equal at some point $x=a$, then this is sufficient to conclude that the limit exists at $x=a.$ 

So, if we have

$$
\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to a^+} f(x) = L,
$$

then we may conclude that

$$
\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L.
$$

For a multivariable function, the situation is not so straightforward. For a function of two variables $f(x,y),$ we may only conclude that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{x}_0} f(x,y) = L,
$$

if we can show that the limit is the same *for all possible paths* on which $\mathbf x$ can approach $\mathbf{x}_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4b46a0a-5b1c-58eb-aa32-dd0ccd57f7a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2482 :tutorial/title "The Definition of a Limit: Single Variable Functions vs. Multivariable Functions"} :step/id #uuid "a9b09430-2391-566d-ac41-6360e135665e" :step/math-academy-id 11094 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125467}} {:db/id 17592186125297 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124457 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124261 :question/id #uuid "56539c63-dd81-57c9-b7d2-18c935953203" :question/math-academy-id "e-3366"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "29610715-333d-5e0c-9328-eec1d45f56ed" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124938} {:db/id 17592186125222} {:db/id 17592186265721} {:db/id 17592186265722} {:db/id 17592186265723} {:db/id 17592186335802} {:db/id 17592186345004} {:db/id 17592186345005} {:db/id 17592186377708} {:db/id 17592186378636} {:db/id 17592186380062} {:db/id 17592186407847} {:db/id 17592186436127} {:db/id 17592186475943} {:db/id 17592186508069} {:db/id 17592186565425} {:db/id 17592186565432}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions"} :step/id #uuid "b6bdeefa-e28b-5e72-8c05-e9f8fb9c7542" :step/math-academy-id 11197} {:db/id 17592186125329 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125754 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we may need to simplify a limit before we can evaluate it. 

For example, let's consider the limit

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,-1)}} \dfrac{x^2+2xy}{xy+2y^2}.
$$

Direct substitution causes this limit to take the indeterminate form $\dfrac 00$ because the numerator and denominator both evaluate to zero at the given point. 

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,-1)}} \dfrac{x^2+2xy}{xy+2y^2} = \dfrac{(2)^2 + 2(2)(-1)}{(2)(-1) + 2(-1)^2} = \dfrac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by factoring the numerator and denominator and then canceling a common factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy+2{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{x(x+2y)}{y(x+2y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{x}{y}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,-1)}} \dfrac{x^2+2xy}{xy+2y^2} = -2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8f5c0d1f-e38c-5cd7-97e2-1aaaac5158b4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2883 :tutorial/title "Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring"} :step/id #uuid "6285e0db-558c-5e11-85ab-0b82dc834963" :step/math-academy-id 15456 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125290}} {:db/id 17592186125466 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124558 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124367 :question/id #uuid "ae167d95-9cfd-5f31-91b1-484becd62677" :question/math-academy-id "e-6239"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7d53554f-6d77-56f9-8950-d8e31a7f4fdb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050225}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125221} {:db/id 17592186125224} {:db/id 17592186265716} {:db/id 17592186265717} {:db/id 17592186265718} {:db/id 17592186265719} {:db/id 17592186345001} {:db/id 17592186345002} {:db/id 17592186345003} {:db/id 17592186407848} {:db/id 17592186407849} {:db/id 17592186436124} {:db/id 17592186436130} {:db/id 17592186508060} {:db/id 17592186534002} {:db/id 17592186565424} {:db/id 17592186565463}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "af7ce556-917b-54ac-a772-adecff1e36f2" :step/math-academy-id 23425 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125291}} {:db/id 17592186125467 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125809 :tutorial/content "However, it is often easy to show that a limit does not exist for a multivariable function. All we have to do is find two paths on which the limit evaluates to different results. 

As an example, let's consider the following limit:

$$
\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)} \dfrac{y}{x+y}
$$

Clearly, direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00.$ Let's compute the limit along the paths $y=x$ and $y=x^2.$ We will see that the limit evaluates to different results on these two paths.

- Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\frac{y}{x+y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{x+x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{y}{x+y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{1+x} \\  & =\frac{0}{1+0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on these two paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \dfrac{y}{x +y} = \text{DNE}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8040690e-6d4c-50ac-8b9f-f92615717816" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3960 :tutorial/title "Proving That a Limit Does Not Exist by Evaluating It Along Different Paths"} :step/id #uuid "29991074-71d2-5a37-a971-5f658f37d3ba" :step/math-academy-id 23498 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125297}}] :activity/title "Limits and Continuity of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124724} {:db/id 17592186125288 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125731 :tutorial/content "We can extend our knowledge of limits to multivariable functions. $$

So, if a function is continuous at $(a,b),$ then the limit can be evaluated by simply plugging $(x,y) = (a,b)$ into the function.

To demonstrate, let's calculate the following limit:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1)}} \dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2}
$$

This function is continuous for all $(x,y)$ with the exception of $(0,0)$ where the denominator vanishes. Since the point $(2,1)$ does not cause the denominator to vanish, we can calculate the limit by substituting $(x,y) = (2,1)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "eccfdda1-288a-5169-adde-a00163fa348f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2480 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a0c271d5-ca3c-5651-a78d-a2b18242c45c" :step/math-academy-id 11087 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125289}} {:db/id 17592186125731 :tutorial/content "We can extend our knowledge of limits to multivariable functions. We'll first consider the two-variable case. 

We denote $\mathbf{x}=(x,y)$ and $\mathbf{x}_0 = (a,b)$ as a particular, fixed vector. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined in some neighborhood of $\mathbf x_0.$ 

Then, the notation

$$
\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{x}_0} f (x,y) = L
$$

means that the value of $f$ can be made as close as we want to $L,$ provided that $\mathbf x$ is sufficiently close to $\mathbf{x}_0.$

A few things to note:

- This definition of a limit also extends to functions of more than two variables in the natural way.

- All of the rules set out by the algebra of limits are valid for functions of several variables.

We say that $f(x,y)$ is **continuous** at $(a,b)$ if

$$
\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (a,b)} f (x,y) = f(a,b).
$$

So, if a function is continuous at $(a,b),$ then the limit can be evaluated by simply plugging $(x,y) = (a,b)$ into the function.

To demonstrate, let's calculate the following limit:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1)}} \dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2}
$$

This function is continuous for all $(x,y)$ with the exception of $(0,0)$ where the denominator vanishes. Since the point $(2,1)$ does not cause the denominator to vanish, we can calculate the limit by substituting $(x,y) = (2,1)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "eccfdda1-288a-5169-adde-a00163fa348f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2480 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125289 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124452 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124256 :question/id #uuid "a5753b43-b288-5cca-a26b-b060917182ab" :question/math-academy-id "e-3330"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1f2ac99b-55b2-5742-81ab-d2961db1250f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050987}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124937} {:db/id 17592186124953} {:db/id 17592186265711} {:db/id 17592186265712} {:db/id 17592186323752} {:db/id 17592186344992} {:db/id 17592186344993} {:db/id 17592186378622} {:db/id 17592186380041} {:db/id 17592186380048} {:db/id 17592186436125} {:db/id 17592186436126} {:db/id 17592186436129} {:db/id 17592186565438}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions at Points of Continuity"} :step/id #uuid "9e271cad-793b-51f0-9124-47a943c42f3e" :step/math-academy-id 11090 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125329}} {:db/id 17592186125329 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125754 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we may need to simplify a limit before we can evaluate it. 

For example, let's consider the limit

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,-1)}} \dfrac{x^2+2xy}{xy+2y^2}.
$$

Direct substitution causes this limit to take the indeterminate form $\dfrac 00$ because the numerator and denominator both evaluate to zero at the given point. 

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,-1)}} \dfrac{x^2+2xy}{xy+2y^2} = \dfrac{(2)^2 + 2(2)(-1)}{(2)(-1) + 2(-1)^2} = \dfrac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by factoring the numerator and denominator and then canceling a common factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy+2{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{x(x+2y)}{y(x+2y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,-1)}\frac{x}{y}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,-1)}} \dfrac{x^2+2xy}{xy+2y^2} = -2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8f5c0d1f-e38c-5cd7-97e2-1aaaac5158b4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2883 :tutorial/title "Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186125732 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a function of a single variable $f(x),$ if the left and right limits both exist and are equal at some point $x=a$, then this is sufficient to conclude that the limit exists at $x=a.$ 

So, if we have

$$
\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to a^+} f(x) = L,
$$

then we may conclude that

$$
\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L.
$$

For a multivariable function, the situation is not so straightforward. For a function of two variables $f(x,y),$ we may only conclude that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{x}_0} f(x,y) = L,
$$

if we can show that the limit is the same *for all possible paths* on which $\mathbf x$ can approach $\mathbf{x}_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4b46a0a-5b1c-58eb-aa32-dd0ccd57f7a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2482 :tutorial/title "The Definition of a Limit: Single Variable Functions vs. Multivariable Functions"} :step/id #uuid "a9b09430-2391-566d-ac41-6360e135665e" :step/math-academy-id 11094 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125467}} {:db/id 17592186125732 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a function of a single variable $f(x),$ if the left and right limits both exist and are equal at some point $x=a$, then this is sufficient to conclude that the limit exists at $x=a.$ 

So, if we have

$$
\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to a^+} f(x) = L,
$$

then we may conclude that

$$
\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L.
$$

For a multivariable function, the situation is not so straightforward. For a function of two variables $f(x,y),$ we may only conclude that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{x}_0} f(x,y) = L,
$$

if we can show that the limit is the same *for all possible paths* on which $\mathbf x$ can approach $\mathbf{x}_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4b46a0a-5b1c-58eb-aa32-dd0ccd57f7a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2482 :tutorial/title "The Definition of a Limit: Single Variable Functions vs. Multivariable Functions"} {:db/id 17592186125467 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125809 :tutorial/content "However, it is often easy to show that a limit does not exist for a multivariable function. All we have to do is find two paths on which the limit evaluates to different results. 

As an example, let's consider the following limit:

$$
\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)} \dfrac{y}{x+y}
$$

Clearly, direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00.$ Let's compute the limit along the paths $y=x$ and $y=x^2.$ We will see that the limit evaluates to different results on these two paths.

- Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\frac{y}{x+y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{x+x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{y}{x+y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{1+x} \\  & =\frac{0}{1+0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on these two paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \dfrac{y}{x +y} = \text{DNE}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8040690e-6d4c-50ac-8b9f-f92615717816" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3960 :tutorial/title "Proving That a Limit Does Not Exist by Evaluating It Along Different Paths"} :step/id #uuid "29991074-71d2-5a37-a971-5f658f37d3ba" :step/math-academy-id 23498 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125297}} {:db/id 17592186125297 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124457 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124261 :question/id #uuid "56539c63-dd81-57c9-b7d2-18c935953203" :question/math-academy-id "e-3366"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "29610715-333d-5e0c-9328-eec1d45f56ed" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124938} {:db/id 17592186125222} {:db/id 17592186265721} {:db/id 17592186265722} {:db/id 17592186265723} {:db/id 17592186335802} {:db/id 17592186345004} {:db/id 17592186345005} {:db/id 17592186377708} {:db/id 17592186378636} {:db/id 17592186380062} {:db/id 17592186407847} {:db/id 17592186436127} {:db/id 17592186475943} {:db/id 17592186508069} {:db/id 17592186565425} {:db/id 17592186565432}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions"} :step/id #uuid "b6bdeefa-e28b-5e72-8c05-e9f8fb9c7542" :step/math-academy-id 11197} {:db/id 17592186125754 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we may need to simplify a limit before we can evaluate it.

$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=2x,$ we have

$$

$$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{\sqrt{xy+2}-2}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}=\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 1+2}-2}{{2}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{\sqrt{xy+2}-2}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{xy+2}-2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)}{({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{xy+2})^{2}-4}{({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{xy-2}{(xy-2)(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{1}{(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$

$$

$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

III. The limit does not exist" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-129409" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d56691a3-bd81-5d30-bd36-57d7d11c4bf9"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5225a54e-55a7-5758-ada6-d6e76ec121f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :question/math-academy-id "q-129401" :question/problem "Determine ${lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & =\frac{{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(1,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,y=0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{0}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,x=1}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}=\text{DNE}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ee66d94f-00d8-5e5e-84ff-35a7175f7dff"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "154cde04-acab-5465-9547-10829d1c2ac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" Consider the picture shown above. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf a$." :question/worked-solution "![](images/b3/b316448c885a20a7ed60871ce0f1a4dc4f77bd4658dc6eda3407fb3c89a088cb.png)

In $\bigtriangleup AHB$ we have

$$
\angle AHB = 90^\circ
$$

, $AH=3$ and $BH=2$. So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB &= \sqrt{AH^{2} + BH^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{3^{2} + 2^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{9 + 4} \\
&= \sqrt{13}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $\mathbf{a}$ is $\sqrt{13}$. Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{1}{\mid a \mid} \cdot a \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}a
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050315} {:db/id 17592186565626} {:db/id 17592186097161 :question/id #uuid "9d05ca0e-131b-5294-8367-1760396e4369" :question/math-academy-id "q-19276" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186096814 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b11642dd-80cc-539c-8c2d-8cdee58e9d3e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector in a Diagram"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ae96c78f-e10d-563b-82af-e2c02160928e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{r}{\sqrt{29}}" :db/id 17592186094940} {:answer/id #uuid "25f7a90e-939a-568d-ba3d-07a616fcb021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{q + r}{5}" :db/id 17592186094941} {:answer/id #uuid "328e6ad2-ef2f-5827-8881-60cdfaebb76b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2q}{\sqrt{13}} + \frac{r}{\sqrt{29}}" :db/id 17592186094942} {:answer/id #uuid "681555fa-cdb3-5281-b943-0cf1eed80c35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(2(q + r))/(\sqrt{73})" :db/id 17592186094943} {:answer/id #uuid "703e463a-8826-5adf-9d3d-36bfd8037d83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{q + r}{\sqrt{13}}" :db/id 17592186094944}] :answer-field/id #uuid "96962338-e491-50f7-b8da-1efc8b69ba83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186094939}] :question/problem "![](images/9d/9dfaf74a497a2fd22428e09a4c26d573e184c9728ccf67f11ebb9d6a2a44f4c6.png)

and has magnitude $20$. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{a+b}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we have to find $\mathbf{a+b}$. According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$ goes from the tail of $\mathbf{a}$ to the head of $\mathbf{b}$:

![](images/32/32c48d8c19fc68fbc172b240ded922f3e2ebc12804411c318ff63fe999aaedcc.png)

To find the unit vector corresponding to $\mathbf{a+b}$, we have to divide by the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{a + b}{\mid a + b \mid}
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the magnitude, first notice that we obtain a right triangle. So, we can use the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}a + b & ^{2} &= & a & ^{2} +\left.\end{vmatrix}b\right|^{2} \\
&= 10^{2} + 20^{2} \\
&= 100 + 400 \\
&= 500
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid \mathbf{a+b} &= \sqrt{500}=10\sqrt{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

and the corresponding unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{a + b}{\mid a + b \mid} \\
&= \frac{1}{10\sqrt{5}}(a + b)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502535} {:db/id 17592186097042 :question/id #uuid "3f0752f9-cfba-5496-a6dc-d603b64b1e81" :question/math-academy-id "q-12184"} {:db/id 17592186097043 :question/id #uuid addition, we can also distribute conjunctions over disjunctions (and vice versa).

- We can distribute a conjunction over a disjunction, as follows:

$$
A \land (B \lor C)  \equiv (A \land B) \lor (A \land C)
$$

- Likewise, we can distribute a disjunction over a conjunction, as follows:

$$
A \lor (B \land C)  \equiv (A \lor B) \land (A \lor C)
$$

{:db/id 17592186158481 :tutorial/content "Just like we can distribute multiplication over addition, we can also distribute conjunctions over disjunctions (and vice versa).

- We can distribute a conjunction over a disjunction, as follows:

$$
A \land (B \lor C)  \equiv (A \land B) \lor (A \land C)
$$

- Likewise, we can distribute a disjunction over a conjunction, as follows:

$$
A \lor (B \land C)  \equiv (A \lor B) \land (A \lor C)
$$

The rules above are called the **distributive laws** for propositional logic. To prove that these laws hold, we can construct truth tables.

"A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $2\sqrt{7}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest." :question/worked-solution "![](images/a8/a8c9778580276589ff7a047ca3c7b620de842efd7b3799a70b6e4484bc5fa0e6.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{7}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{7})^{2} & =-2(1)^{3}+C \\ C & =14+2 \\ C & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=16-2{x}^{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =16-2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =16-2{x}^{3} \\ 2{x}^{3} & =16 \\ {x}^{3} & =8 \\ x & =2\,m.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365350 :question/id #uuid "a7407b0b-36b6-5f0d-b3ce-2c90d7096c04" :question/math-academy-id "q-163573"} {:db/id 17592186365357 :question/id #uuid "7b27beee-357c-5af3-8233-0a884c5b276c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163574" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179692 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "093a897b-2422-5e5b-b713-c8cd61a702dc" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Points Where a Particle Is at Instantaneous Rest"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c2269031-3808-5832-884f-e8b8017c9c9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x=\pm \frac{4}{3}\,m" :db/id 17592186365359} {:answer/id #uuid "4a6c3024-fa5b-5f46-969f-814b049ab789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x=\pm \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{15}\,m" :db/id 17592186365360} {:answer/id #uuid "6bcd61a1-599b-5b2c-85f2-4b2c81af9b25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x=\pm 4\sqrt{5}\,m" :db/id 17592186365361} {:answer/id #uuid "67d1e270-938d-5f31-9382-769f0bc70e6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x=3\sqrt{5}\,m" :db/id 17592186365362} {:answer/id #uuid "0e3ceed1-cddd-5143-b1a9-6164a52295df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x=\sqrt{15}\,m" :db/id 17592186365363}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "4a6c3024-fa5b-5f46-969f-814b049ab789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x=\pm \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{15}\,m" :db/id 17592186365360} :answer-field/id #uuid "657f8a9e-940d-51df-b4a4-eb87c6fcb879" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186365358}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $6x\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $4\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest." :question/worked-solution "![](images/fa/fa329a81ac533c3ab4bfd9ca6fb5b2ef81ff4e29fb8ff7f030c5e04952d9448d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-6x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-3{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-3{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-3(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+12 \\ C & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=20-3{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

"A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\sqrt{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=6\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $9\,m,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/b0/b052a65fb0dbcc14a5d359b693beafdf5da3f4bbe1e10f006c315e8168340d5c.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\sqrt{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\sqrt{x}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\sqrt{x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k\sqrt{x})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}(0)^{3/2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+18.
$$

Finally, since $v=6\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=9\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+18 \\ \frac{1}{2}(6\sqrt{6})^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}(9)^{3/2}+18 \\ 108 & =18k+18 \\ 18k & =90 \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365246 :question/id #uuid "89d922d3-34d3-536f-bab1-5d011a22c471" :question/math-academy-id "q-163500"} {:db/id 17592186365267 :question/id #uuid "850e5b75-4192-55dd-95c1-60411426a4e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163550" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6dde8744-6fdc-5e2d-b736-074a3c935944" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186365269} {:answer/id #uuid "2e60c10f-bfb0-5906-b010-ebfe71f74caa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186365270} {:answer/id #uuid "e931fb28-3c65-5cdd-bd58-88282355e37a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186365271} {:answer/id #uuid "dd1e58b1-199d-5fb2-88e7-6318356fb651" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186365272} {:answer/id #uuid "59060e22-55d4-5810-9281-aa0ce058e469" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186365273}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365270} :answer-field/id #uuid "a4d2807e-e4a2-58a8-bf6a-268785e8822d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365268}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=3\sqrt{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}(3\sqrt{2})^{2} \\ 18-9k & =0 \\ 9k & =18 \\ k & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365274 :question/id #uuid "346646b9-04ff-58cb-a1cc-6c9b42073112" :question/math-academy-id "q-163551"} {:db/id 17592186365295 :question/id #uuid "08ac1e00-dffa-559e-955d-dfbbd3b1b61a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163558"} {:db/id 17592186365329 :question/id #uuid "19e94881-dc11-5b6a-8172-59477ad89f5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-163565" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8ebcf16d-17e2-521f-84af-8c80fc770e40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186365331} {:answer/id #uuid "f51a32aa-8b15-5397-a3a9-3d850bb58c1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186365332} {:answer/id #uuid "3bea1d31-74b4-5ddf-8bc9-1bd6d0bd85b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186365333} {:answer/id #uuid "b4036230-717e-5222-ab98-3a9fdf09553e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186365334} {:answer/id #uuid "8832e1f0-db88-5028-8c7f-f4ff514e3d16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186365335}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365334} :answer-field/id #uuid "9f1e0c06-6d19-533b-b17a-f929a1be5595" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365330}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(10+kx)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(10+kx).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(10+kx).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int -(10+kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=12\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(12)^{2} & =-10(0)-\frac{k(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =72\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=72-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{15}\,m/s$ when $x=4\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =72-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{15})^{2} & =72-10(4)-\frac{k(4)^{2}}{2} \\ 30 & =72-40-8k \\ 8k & =2 \\ k & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186489194 :question/id #uuid "2593d620-c288-5ff9-965a-23a30b035fd9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163498"} {:db/id 17592186489279 :question/id #uuid
